artworks.title: Heracles at Pholus (Attic black-figured hydria)
artworks.description: This Attic black-figured hydria (a calpis-type water vessel, 24.5 cm high) depicts the hospitable reception that defines Pholus in myth: the centaur welcoming Heracles to his Arcadian cave on the hero's Erymanthian-boar quest. Pholus is rendered as a typical centaur with a man's torso joined to a horse's body, greeting his guest in the moment before the fateful opening of the communal centaur wine-jar. The scene crystallizes the friendship between host and hero that Apollodorus records (Bibliotheca 2.5.4) and which would end in Pholus's accidental death by one of Heracles' poisoned arrows. Now in the Louvre, Paris (accession MNE 940).

artworks.title: Heracles, Pholus and the Centaurs (black-figured skyphos)
artworks.description: A small Corinthian black-figured skyphos (drinking cup, 9.7 cm high) attributed to the artist conventionally named the Pholoe Painter after this very subject. It shows the climactic battle that erupts after the communal wine-jar is opened at Pholus's cave: Heracles drives off the wild centaurs who swarm at the scent of the wine, the episode in which an errant arrow accidentally wounds Chiron and ultimately costs the gentle Pholus his life. Found at Corinth, the vase places Pholus at the center of the centaur-war cycle so often depicted in archaic Greek art. Now in the Louvre, Paris (accession MNC 677 / L 63).

artworks.title: Herakles and Pholos (Attic Red-Figure Oinochoe)
artworks.description: An Attic red-figure oinochoe of about 500–490 BC shows Heracles with Pholus in the cave hospitality scene that opens the Pholoe adventure. Where black-figure predecessors fixed the silhouette of host and guest, the red-figure painter gives the civilized centaur and the hero clearer gesture and drapery on the brink of the wine-jar disaster. National Archaeological Museum, Madrid.

artworks.title: Pholos Drawing Wine for Herakles (Attic Black-Figure Lekythos)
artworks.description: On this Attic black-figure lekythos attributed to the Gela Painter, Pholus draws wine from the communal jar for his guest Heracles — the courteous act that, in Apollodorus, releases the scent that maddens the wild centaurs and ends in Pholus's own death by a poisoned arrow. The vase isolates the hospitable moment before the battle, making the gentle centaur the focus rather than the melee. Museo Archeologico Regionale, Palermo (NI 1904).

artworks.title: Herakles and Pholos (Attic Black-Figure Lekythos)
artworks.description: A black-figure lekythos in the Walters Art Museum (48.229) attributed to the Beldam Painter stages another version of Heracles' visit to Pholus — one of the parerga that vase-painters loved beside the canonical labours. Draped figures and the centaur host evoke the wine-sharing that turns fatal on Mount Pholoe. The vessel is a compact Classical-period witness to Pholus as the hospitable counterpart of the wilder Centaurs.
